A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AB-MCTS research. All 16 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2 support comparison, including equations, figures, and v2 Appendices A–D. Material moved from v1's main text into v2's appendices was matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original CodeContest experiments and evaluations on three MLE-Bench competitions, including performance curves in Figures 4–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original evaluations on LiveCodeBench, CodeContest, ARC-AGI, and three MLE-Bench competitions, together with search-behavior analyses.

M1.justification: Appendix B adds a multi-LLM extension with an adaptive generator-selection step at every expansion. Thompson sampling selects an LLM using generator-specific score histories and mixed-model or independent-prior posteriors. This introduces a substantial new procedural component while retaining the original single-LLM algorithms; the extension is not experimentally evaluated.

E1.justification: V2 adds recent competitive-programming problems from LiveCodeBench and visual-rule induction through code generation on ARC-AGI. These expand the represented data and task requirements beyond v1's CodeContest and three retained MLE-Bench competitions.

E2.justification: Sequential refinement becomes an evaluated baseline; v1 discussed it conceptually but did not report its performance. For MLE-Bench specifically, v2 also adds standard MCTS alongside repeated sampling, substantially strengthening the comparison against alternative search strategies.

E3.justification: The reported DeepSeek-V3 CodeContest temperature changes from 1.5 to 1.0 and its main evaluation budget from 512 to 128 calls. MLE-Bench switches from DeepSeek-V3 to GPT-4o. V2 also changes the stated coding prompt-template source and introduces ARC-AGI Pass@2 evaluation with an additional 512-call scaling experiment.

E4.justification: V2 adds quantitative search-depth/width analyses (Figures 5 and 9), qualitative MLE-Bench search-tree comparisons (Figures 6 and 11), and an extended-budget ARC-AGI scaling study (Figure 7). V1 contains benchmark performance curves but lacks these search-behavior diagnostics and case studies.

E5.justification: V2 first specifies five runs for LiveCodeBench, three for CodeContest and ARC-AGI, and one for MLE-Bench. Its coding/ARC plots add individual-run results and 95% confidence intervals at the maximum main budget. V1 supplies neither explicit run counts nor comparable uncertainty reporting; this does not establish an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive LiveCodeBench and ARC-AGI results and replaces the MLE-Bench results with GPT-4o evaluations, omitting the earlier AB-MCTS-A Gaussian results there. The reported GPT-4o CodeContest ordering also changes: v1 places Beta above M, whereas v2 Table 1 reports 40.6 for M versus 40.4 for Beta. Changed protocols prevent treating these as controlled cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds a formal multi-generator setting, generator-specific observation sets, and statistical assumptions grouping rewards by their generating LLM. This extends the modeled setting beyond node-level selection. The original single-LLM mixed-model equations and Gaussian/Beta updates are retained in Appendix A; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contributions—adaptive branching, the two single-LLM variants, and improved inference-time search—remain. V2's conclusion drops v1's suggested applicability beyond LLM answer generation to broader stochastic or infinite-action problems, producing a limited narrowing of the stated scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting search shape and task-dependent baseline strengths to adaptive exploration and refinement. It replaces v1's budget-based preference for particular MLE variants with an adaptability argument for AB-MCTS-M. It also removes the prior-tuning limitation, argues that accumulated observations should reduce prior sensitivity, and adds the limitation of measuring cost only through API-call counts.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds concrete PyMC examples for the mixed model and GEN-node prediction. Appendix C supplies benchmark selection and prompt information and discloses a single H100 GPU with a one-hour execution limit per MLE candidate. These materially expand implementation and reproducibility documentation; the original prior values are largely retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds references including Chollet's ARC work, Schaeffer et al., PyMC, and Hypothesis Search, while removing several background references. The broad research positioning remains, but the progressive-widening comparison now emphasizes the statistical information available because branches share an LLM generator.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and compresses the introduction, related work, and method exposition. The standalone preliminaries are integrated into the method section, while extended preliminaries and mathematical details move into Appendix A. New analysis sections and organized appendices substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds two summary tables, search-shape plots, empirical tree visualizations, and an extended-budget plot. Performance figures are reorganized by model and benchmark and gain uncertainty insets. Method diagrams are revised, and equations and MLE plots are relocated. Figure 11 explicitly repeats Figure 6's Pizza tree alongside additional examples.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's empirical support: it evaluates sequential refinement, directly examines search behavior, and reports repeated-run uncertainty. Broader evaluations also expose conditions where baselines win, making the central claims easier to assess. Added implementation examples improve reproducibility. Changed settings and narrower MLE variant coverage limit continuity, and the prior-sensitivity argument remains untested, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in comparative evidence and transparency.
